Family Health

Menopause and insomnia: finding a treatment that fits

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Poor sleep during perimenopause or after menopause can leave you exhausted and worried about the next night. Hormonal changes may be part of the picture, but they are not the only explanation. A useful plan considers both menopause symptoms and the patterns that keep insomnia going.

Sleep can change before periods stop completely

During perimenopause, ovarian hormone levels fluctuate and menstrual patterns change. Menopause is generally recognised after 12 months without a period when there is no other explanation and hormonal contraception is not obscuring the pattern. The time afterwards is postmenopause. Sleep symptoms can begin during the transition rather than waiting for that anniversary.

Trouble sleeping is common at this stage, but not everyone develops an insomnia disorder. Estimates of how many people are affected vary because studies measure different things: occasional disrupted sleep, night sweats and persistent insomnia are not identical. Your symptoms and their effect on daily life matter more than whether you fit a quoted percentage.

Insomnia is about difficulty and daytime impact

Insomnia can mean difficulty falling asleep, repeated waking with difficulty returning to sleep, or waking earlier than you want despite having enough opportunity to sleep. Some people lie awake for 30 minutes or more or sleep fewer than six hours, but neither number is a universal diagnostic cutoff. Sleep needs and schedules differ.

You may feel unrefreshed, tired, sleepy, irritable or anxious during the day. Concentration, memory and task completion can suffer, and mistakes or accidents may become more likely. Worrying constantly about the next night can add to the problem. Headaches or stomach upset may accompany poor sleep, but should not automatically be attributed to it.

Symptoms at least three nights a week for three months or longer are part of the definition of chronic insomnia. Shorter episodes still deserve help if they interfere with your life. You do not need to wait three months before asking for support.

Hormones and night sweats can contribute

Changes in oestrogen and progesterone can influence sleep and the body’s temperature regulation. Progesterone-related pathways may affect sleepiness, but it is too simple to describe one hormone as an on-off sleep switch or assume that a blood hormone level explains every bad night.

Hot flushes and night sweats can wake you, leave bedding uncomfortable and make it difficult to settle again. You may feel a sudden wave of heat or notice a racing heartbeat. This is not adequately explained by a universal burst of adrenaline from a rapid hormone drop. Treating troublesome vasomotor symptoms may help sleep, while persistent insomnia may still need its own treatment.

Look for contributors beyond menopause

Work, family pressures, relationship stress, anxiety or depression can disrupt sleep. Pain, reflux, needing to urinate, thyroid problems and other health conditions may also contribute. Age can change sleep patterns, but being over 60 does not make disabling sleeplessness inevitable or untreatable.

Snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, gasping or marked daytime sleepiness can suggest sleep apnoea. An uncomfortable urge to move the legs in the evening may suggest restless legs. These conditions need assessment rather than more time in bed. Sleep-disordered breathing becomes more common after menopause.

Review medicines and supplements, especially anything started or changed recently. Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, late heavy meals, shift work and travel across time zones can also affect sleep. Do not stop a prescribed medicine abruptly; ask whether its dose, timing, interactions or an alternative could be relevant.

A sleep diary can make the appointment more useful

For one or two weeks, note bedtime, approximate time to fall asleep, awakenings, final waking, naps and daytime tiredness. Include night sweats, caffeine or alcohol, medicines and any events that seem related. An estimate is enough; repeatedly watching the clock can make sleep anxiety worse.

Your clinician may ask about mood, breathing during sleep, pain and your menstrual history and perform an examination. Blood tests are chosen for a suspected problem, such as thyroid disease, rather than automatically being needed for every sleep complaint. An overnight sleep study is usually considered when another sleep disorder is suspected; it is not the routine next step whenever insomnia has no obvious cause.

Make the bedroom comfortable, dark and quiet

Aim for a room that feels comfortably cool, with bedding you can adjust if you become hot. Around 18°C is sometimes suggested as a starting point, but there is no single required temperature and colder is not always better. Your comfort, season and home conditions matter.

Reduce unnecessary light from lamps, clocks and screens, and silence avoidable alerts or noise. If a clock encourages repeated checking, turn it away. You do not need to buy a sleep gadget or special product to begin. A dark, quiet environment supports sleep but may not resolve a persistent insomnia disorder by itself.

Plan food, drinks and nicotine around sleep

A large late meal may worsen reflux or discomfort when you lie down. Try allowing time after dinner before bed. A small snack may suit some people, but a glass of milk is not a required treatment and should fit your tolerance and dietary needs.

Reduce caffeine later in the day and notice how sensitive you are to it. Nicotine is stimulating; help to stop smoking can support broader health as well as sleep. Alcohol may make you drowsy at first, but it can fragment later sleep and worsen breathing problems, so it is not a reliable sleep aid.

Stay normally hydrated during the day without using water as a replacement for lost sleep. Large drinks immediately before bed may increase toilet trips. If thirst or frequent urination is excessive or new, mention it at your appointment rather than simply restricting fluids.

Use a wind-down routine and a steady schedule

Gentle stretching, relaxed breathing, quiet reading or a calming activity can help you transition out of the day. Yoga may suit some people if comfortable, but relaxation does not have to look a particular way. Regular daytime activity and daylight can also help support your sleep rhythm.

Keep a reasonably consistent wake-up time and go to bed when sleepy. Avoid compensating for every difficult night by spending much longer in bed or sleeping late the next morning. If your natural schedule shifts earlier, discuss an achievable adjustment that still leaves enough sleep opportunity. The aim is a workable rhythm, not rigidly forcing yourself to sleep on command.

Ask about cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia

Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, CBT-I, is usually the first treatment for chronic insomnia. It addresses the thoughts and habits that keep sleeplessness going, including the cycle of anxiety about sleep. It goes beyond a list of sleep-hygiene tips and can be delivered in person, remotely or through suitable digital programmes.

A programme may include stimulus control, relaxation and a carefully adjusted sleep schedule. Some approaches temporarily limit time in bed to improve sleep efficiency, but do not copy a severe sleep-restriction plan without appropriate guidance, especially if you are already dangerously sleepy.

Menopause-specific CBT is another option for sleep problems associated with menopause symptoms. It can be used alongside hormone therapy or when hormones are unsuitable or unwanted. Ask which approach fits your symptoms and how to access it locally.

Treat menopause symptoms with an individual plan

Hormone replacement therapy, HRT, can help troublesome hot flushes and night sweats and may improve sleep when those symptoms are the main driver. It is not a guaranteed cure for every insomnia problem. Choice depends on symptoms, age, medical history, preferences and the balance of benefits and risks.

If you have a uterus, systemic oestrogen usually needs a progestogen to protect the uterine lining. A vaginal treatment for local dryness is a different treatment and should not be expected to resolve night sweats or insomnia. Discuss your exact symptoms rather than asking only to “balance hormones”.

For some suitable people in perimenopause who also need contraception, a combined hormonal contraceptive may be an alternative. It is not a general low-dose sleeping medicine and is not taken at the same time as HRT. HRT itself does not prevent pregnancy; contraception needs a separate discussion.

Antidepressants, melatonin and sleeping medicines have different roles

An antidepressant may be appropriate for depression or anxiety, and selected medicines can also help vasomotor symptoms in particular circumstances. That does not mean everyone with menopause insomnia should take a low-dose antidepressant. Some medicines can worsen sleep or cause other effects, so the reason for prescribing matters.

Melatonin helps signal sleep timing, but it is not a proven universal treatment for chronic insomnia or a way to restore ovarian hormones. In the UK it is prescribed mainly for short-term sleep problems in people aged 55 and over, with some specialist uses. Availability and indications differ between countries. Discuss the formulation, interactions and next-day effects before using it.

Sleeping tablets or sedating over-the-counter products may sometimes be used briefly, but can cause daytime impairment, falls or dependence, depending on the product. They do not replace investigation of persistent symptoms or CBT-I. Avoid combining sedatives, alcohol and herbal sleep products without advice.

Protect daytime safety and review what is working

Frequent or late naps can reduce the drive to sleep at night and are not a default treatment for chronic insomnia. If you need daytime rest because of significant sleepiness, discuss timing and safety with your clinician. Do not drive or operate machinery when sleepy, and do not rely on caffeine or a glass of water to make that safe.

Agree on a review date and a few useful goals, such as fewer long awakenings, less night-sweat disruption or better daytime functioning. If sleep is affecting mood, work or daily responsibilities, say so. Persistent symptoms after one approach do not mean you must accept them: the diagnosis, menopause treatment or sleep plan may need adjustment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CBT-I is usually the first treatment for persistent insomnia, with assessment of other sleep disorders when indicated.

Menopause treatments can help associated symptoms; they are chosen individually rather than prescribed as universal sleep remedies.

How BeMama can help

Use a short sleep diary to connect awakenings, night sweats, daytime symptoms and medicines before your review.

When to seek help

Do not drive when sleepy. Seek care when symptoms impair daily life, or when snoring, breathing pauses, severe mood symptoms or medication effects suggest an additional problem.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Trouble sleeping can begin before periods stop.
  • Six hours or 30 minutes awake is not a diagnosis by itself.
  • Night sweats, insomnia and sleep apnoea may need different care.
  • Frequent naps and alcohol can worsen the sleep pattern.
  • Treatments should be reviewed against symptoms and daytime function.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to wait until menopause is confirmed to ask for help?

No. Sleep symptoms can begin during perimenopause, and support or treatment can be considered before periods stop completely.

Does sleeping less than six hours prove I have insomnia?

No. Diagnosis considers difficulty sleeping despite adequate opportunity, frequency, duration and daytime impact. A single hour count is not enough.

Are all night-time awakenings caused by low oestrogen?

No. Hot flushes can contribute, but stress, medicines, pain, reflux, sleep apnoea and other problems may also matter.

Will everyone with insomnia need a sleep study?

No. A sleep study is generally used when another sleep disorder is suspected. A history, diary and targeted assessment often guide insomnia care.

Is 18°C the only correct bedroom temperature?

No. It is a possible starting point, not a requirement. Aim for comfortable coolness and adjustable bedding rather than making yourself cold.

Should I take frequent naps after a poor night?

Not as a routine insomnia treatment. Frequent or late naps can reduce night-time sleep drive. Discuss significant daytime sleepiness and avoid driving when sleepy.

Is CBT-I just advice to avoid screens?

No. It is a structured treatment addressing sleep-related thoughts, behaviours and scheduling. Sleep-hygiene changes are only one part of care.

Will HRT definitely cure my insomnia?

No. It may help when hot flushes or night sweats disrupt sleep, but persistent insomnia may also need CBT-I or treatment of another condition.

Can I use HRT and the combined pill together for sleep?

No. The combined pill may be an alternative for suitable people who need contraception, but is not taken at the same time as HRT. Ask for an individual plan.

Is melatonin a harmless cure for menopause sleep problems?

No. It has selected uses, possible interactions and next-day effects, and is not a universal treatment for chronic insomnia. Check the indication and local product with a clinician.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
